newsitem.title: UK: As Deng dies, business thrives in London Chinatown.
newsitem.headline: As Deng dies, business thrives in London Chinatown.

text.p: London's chaotic Chinatown met the death of Deng Xiaoping with the cool pragmatism of a Confucian proverb on Thursday, saying old men must die and profits live on.
From young to old, the merchants put their future prosperity before any sentimentality about doctrines past as they shucked and stacked the produce in London's own little China.

"A man that old has to die. New blood must come up ," said Patrick Tsang, a 50-year-old shopkeeper. "China was fortunate to have him but there was no energy left. Everyone must die and it was surely his turn."
Deng, in the advanced stages of Parkinson's disease, died of complications from lung infection on Wednesday night. He was 92.
As mourning began in a placid Beijing, so too in London, the diaspora greeted news of his death with complete calm.
"He has died?" asked 25-year-old Siu Koon Ho, a tourist from Hong Kong drawn by the sights and smells of home as he meandered through the food-filled jumble that is London's Chinatown.
"For so long we didn't see him, except in the same old photos, that I sometimes thought he was dead already and nobody had told us," he said.
"Now it really has happened -- but still I feel nothing."
Lau Wai Yuen, a graphic artist dressed in vinyl, sunglasses and a feather-boa scarf, said the death of China's paramount leader was utterly divorced from his life of flair and fun.
"I'm not remotely interested in history. He was just another old man," said 24-year-old Wai Yuen. "I simply don't care."
Indeed it fell to the elders to pay respects to the elfin-faced man who ushered in "socialism with Chinese characteristics", even if they, too, seemed fixated on the finances.

"I would give him 75 percent. He has been good and he has been bad, like any other leader, but he was old enough to die," said Leslie Ng, who spent the night of Deng's death at a London soccer game with four families of ardent, rain-drenched fans.
Amid stacks of ginger and jack fruit, chilli and chestnuts, Ng said it was prices, not policy, that made the world go round.

"Deng made great economic strides and that will carry on," said Ng, who nimbly compared growth rates in China with those of Europe and counterposed complex U.S. trade policy towards Cuba and China as if he were juggling a couple of lychees.

"We have to admit the guy is physically not on the planet any more, gone, and turn all eyes on today's leaders. Economics is the policy of the 21st century and Deng's policy of capitalistic socialism has to carry on. There is no other way."
Yet Andre Cheong, who runs the New Loon Moon Supermarket, said Deng's death could affect his business, which is heavily reliant on imports from both Hong Kong and China.

"We will wait and see until the new regime comes in to find out what kind of people we're dealing with. At present, I have very little respect for China -- she has everything to offer but can deliver nothing because of her policies," he said.

"Deng put forward some good ideas, fine. But someone has to change the political system otherwise China will end up a Third World country run by entrepreneurial Europeans and Asians. It's such a waste," said Cheong, who came to London in 1978.
It fell to retired Cambodian Ken Tran to honour Deng's place in history, though he too planned neither tears nor ceremony.
"Deng was in bed for a long time but this was still a very great man," he said. "Forget Mao. In one hundred years, people will recognise that Deng is the only man in Chinese history.
"Nobody is perfect. But so far, Deng Xiaoping is the best."
